description.value: There is a F/X risk of the Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) against USD because the vast majority of FI Own Loan to final beneficiaries are likely to be provided in IDR as it is the case for a typical corporate loan to domestic borrowers; however, GCF funding (Guarantee) is provided only in USD. As the GCF Credit Guarantee is denominated and made available in USD, FIs (as guarantee recipients) may be exposed to a currency mismatch risk related to the currency of defaulted debt service amounts under the FI Own Loan (in IDR, but this currency mismatch risk is limited to the case where IDR appreciates against USD.

mitigation.value:
The GCF Credit Guarantee will be designed in a way which the foregoing F/X risk would be partially absorbed by the GCF and F/X risk not absorbed by GCF is borne by local FIs.
F/X risk will be regularly monitored and managed by a professional Guarantee Advisor who would be employed by KDB.

description.value: The GCF proceeds under the programme can also be utilised to support anti-terrorist activities, money laundering or prohibited activities policies by FIs or the final beneficiaries. Additionally, this risk of a failure to meet international standards with respect to preventing money laundering and/or financing of terrorism can present problems, such as obstacles to financial flows and/or implementation and/or payment processing.

mitigation.value:
The programme under Component 1 is supporting credit guarantees with local FIs, who will provide FI Own Loans to the final beneficiaries. As FIs were or will be selected through the proper capacity assessment by KDB including AML/CFT (KYC) assessment, final beneficiaries must also undergo due diligence according to the Sub-Project Loan Agreement between the FI and the final beneficiary. Then, it is considered that such related risk has been substantially mitigated.
Also, Indonesia has the national regulatory system to monitor relevant issues of the financial institutions under the purview of central bank. Moreover, the potential Executing Entity under Component 1 has an internal regulation and policy about their investment activities, so the final beneficiaries’ activities under the programme will be properly screened and monitored.
Under Components 2 and 3, AML/CFT assessment on the Executing Entity (ACE) is already completed by KDB, and the activities of implementing entities will be monitored if they are in line with the ACE’s internal regulations agreed by KDB. Reporting of complaints and allegations of impropriety, wrongdoing etc., are
conducted by PIU (Programme Implementation Unit) for Business Coordination and Sustainability under KDB Supervision, which will be established in each local FI under Component 3.

expected_labels: Indonesia is in need of urgent actions to address gradually deteriorating climate change impacts and their consequences. The climate-vulnerable archipelagic state submitted its nationally determined contribution (NDC) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) with a strong willingness to transition towards a low-carbon and climate-resilient pathway. The NDC of Indonesia recognises energy efficiency as one of its key mitigation actions. While Indonesia attributes 65.43% of the total greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to the energy sector, the market penetration of energy efficient technologies and the ensuing energy savings have been long hampered by a range of barriers, such as access to finance, regulatory challenges, and a lack of capacity and awareness amongst relevant stakeholders. In addition,since the Coronavirus Disease (COVID-19) outbreak and spread, the state budget and relevant stimulus measures in the neediest areas have brought the agenda of energy efficiency and conservation back in terms of priority. Surrounded by further setbacks from the pandemic and related budget deficits, an international-level intervention in the urgent, but deprioritised area is more important than ever. The Programme entitled “Supporting Innovative Mechanisms for Industrial Energy Efficiency Financing in Indonesia with Lessons for Replication in the other ASEAN Member States,” hereafter “Programme,” will support Indonesia and its neighbouring ASEAN members to re-focus on climate actions amid the postpandemic recovery era, strengthening the foundation for the NDC achievement and the national alignment with the Paris Agreement eventually. The Programme, therefore, shall support Indonesia and other ASEAN countries to be ready to drive a lowcarbon development pathway with enhanced energy efficiency and conservation performance, addressing three chronic barriers – i.e., financial, regulatory, and technical barriers, which are all interlinked with a vicious circle of implementation failures of similar precedents. This initiative pays special attention to the three challenges, regarding them as the three entry points of intervention and designing three components accordingly as below. The Programme proposes a solution package of innovative energy efficiency financing schemes equipped with de-risking mechanisms, a supportive regulatory framework, and technical assistance.

description.value: There is a F/X risk of the Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) against USD because the vast majority of FI Own Loan to final beneficiaries are likely to be provided in IDR as it is the case for a typical corporate loan to domestic borrowers; however, GCF funding (Guarantee) is provided only in USD. As the GCF Credit Guarantee is denominated and made available in USD, FIs (as guarantee recipients) may be exposed to a currency mismatch risk related to the currency of defaulted debt service amounts under the FI Own Loan (in IDR, but this currency mismatch risk is limited to the case where IDR appreciates against USD.

mitigation.value:
The GCF Credit Guarantee will be designed in a way which the foregoing F/X risk would be partially absorbed by the GCF and F/X risk not absorbed by GCF is borne by local FIs.
F/X risk will be regularly monitored and managed by a professional Guarantee Advisor who would be employed by KDB.

description.value: The GCF proceeds under the programme can also be utilised to support anti-terrorist activities, money laundering or prohibited activities policies by FIs or the final beneficiaries. Additionally, this risk of a failure to meet international standards with respect to preventing money laundering and/or financing of terrorism can present problems, such as obstacles to financial flows and/or implementation and/or payment processing.

mitigation.value:
The programme under Component 1 is supporting credit guarantees with local FIs, who will provide FI Own Loans to the final beneficiaries. As FIs were or will be selected through the proper capacity assessment by KDB including AML/CFT (KYC) assessment, final beneficiaries must also undergo due diligence according to the Sub-Project Loan Agreement between the FI and the final beneficiary. Then, it is considered that such related risk has been substantially mitigated.
Also, Indonesia has the national regulatory system to monitor relevant issues of the financial institutions under the purview of central bank. Moreover, the potential Executing Entity under Component 1 has an internal regulation and policy about their investment activities, so the final beneficiaries’ activities under the programme will be properly screened and monitored.
Under Components 2 and 3, AML/CFT assessment on the Executing Entity (ACE) is already completed by KDB, and the activities of implementing entities will be monitored if they are in line with the ACE’s internal regulations agreed by KDB. Reporting of complaints and allegations of impropriety, wrongdoing etc., are
conducted by PIU (Programme Implementation Unit) for Business Coordination and Sustainability under KDB Supervision, which will be established in each local FI under Component 3.

description.value: A potential technical and operation risk might be caused by a lack of knowledge and competence of end beneficiaries – mainly industrial enterprise owners – surrounded by the least-developed energy efficiency market circumstances. Especially, industrial enterprises ought to adopt themselves to change into energy efficient equipment and technologies. The change necessarily requires enterprises to redefine the operation and management (O&M) process as per modification and/or replacement of technical methodology and operational mechanism.

mitigation.value:
The eligibility criteria require local FIs and their borrowers (end beneficiaries) to carry out a technical assessment on underlying projects so that any potential technical and operational risk attributable to unfamiliarity and a lack of skill and knowledge could be minimised as much as possible.
The set criteria further require demonstration of a concrete O&M plan over the borrowing lifespan in order to ensure the energy efficiency system optimisation and energy saving results accordingly.
As per request from partner FIs, the Programme provides support for a technical assessment of the vulnerable group of local beneficiaries under Component 3.

description.value: The GCF Guarantee Facility of Component 1 would be directly exposed to the risk by its nature, up to a preagreed guarantee coverage ratio. As typically seen in a credit guarantee or insurance product, the guarantor could be also exposed to any credit risk attributable to information-asymmetry.

mitigation.value:
Shortlisting and selection of local FIs takes the credit rating and relevant reputation into account. In particular, SMI and IIF, under the current discussion, are reputable private financial institutions in Indonesia and their respective credit ratings are equivalent or close to sovereign rating of the country. As such, it does not foresee the credit risk to be potentially material.
As for the FI Own Loan to be backed by the GCF guarantee Cover, the FI would share any credit risk of the relevant borrowers up to the residual portion under the guaranteed FI Own Loan. With the said mechanism, any credit risk of the final beneficiary exposed to relevant FI is not insignificant, thus the moral hazard risk to be less likely to occur. 
What is more, equity injection from a final beneficiary could be told as another mitigation measure against any credit risk of borrowers.

description.value: There is a F/X risk of the Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) against USD because the vast majority of FI Own Loan to final beneficiaries are likely to be provided in IDR as it is the case for a typical corporate loan to domestic borrowers; however, GCF funding (Guarantee) is provided only in USD. As the GCF Credit Guarantee is denominated and made available in USD, FIs (as guarantee recipients) may be exposed to a currency mismatch risk related to the currency of defaulted debt service amounts under the FI Own Loan (in IDR, but this currency mismatch risk is limited to the case where IDR appreciates against USD.

mitigation.value:
The GCF Credit Guarantee will be designed in a way which the foregoing F/X risk would be partially absorbed by the GCF and F/X risk not absorbed by GCF is borne by local FIs.
F/X risk will be regularly monitored and managed by a professional Guarantee Advisor who would be employed by KDB.

description.value: The programme entails multi-dimensional and multi-level legal and contractual arrangements with multiple parties, which might carry a potential legal risk in association with legality or validity and enforceability of any agreement or contract. Furthermore, dis-alignment amongst agreements and contracts governed by different jurisdictions might be another potential legal risk.

mitigation.value:
In order to avoid a potential legal risk arisen by jurisdiction discrepancy, definitive agreements where KDB is a contracting party – i.e., FAA, Guarantee Agreement, and TA Service Agreement – are to be universally governed under English Law and potent disputes are to be resolved by arbitration administered by the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) in accordance with the SIAC Arbitration Rules. This is to be incorporated in the agreements.
On the other hand, all the Sub-Project Loan Agreements to be entered between a FI and each borrower are likely to be governed by the Indonesian law – the host country law. That implies that all the sub-transactions are standard corporate loan financing, which are the core business areas of local FIs with an extensive track record over decades. In that regard, the occurrence of any legal risk, potentially caused by jurisdictional discrepancy seems marginal; and even if a potential risk occurs, local FIs are deemed capable enough to tackle the legal disputes by themselves as a contacting party versed in the local legal process.
In addition, all legal agreements in the programme will be carried out with support and advice from qualified independent legal advisors, which will minimize the legal issues and controversies.

description.value: The GCF proceeds under the programme can also be utilised to support anti-terrorist activities, money laundering or prohibited activities policies by FIs or the final beneficiaries. Additionally, this risk of a failure to meet international standards with respect to preventing money laundering and/or financing of terrorism can present problems, such as obstacles to financial flows and/or implementation and/or payment processing.

mitigation.value:
The programme under Component 1 is supporting credit guarantees with local FIs, who will provide FI Own Loans to the final beneficiaries. As FIs were or will be selected through the proper capacity assessment by KDB including AML/CFT (KYC) assessment, final beneficiaries must also undergo due diligence according to the Sub-Project Loan Agreement between the FI and the final beneficiary. Then, it is considered that such related risk has been substantially mitigated.
Also, Indonesia has the national regulatory system to monitor relevant issues of the financial institutions under the purview of central bank. Moreover, the potential Executing Entity under Component 1 has an internal regulation and policy about their investment activities, so the final beneficiaries’ activities under the programme will be properly screened and monitored.
Under Components 2 and 3, AML/CFT assessment on the Executing Entity (ACE) is already completed by KDB, and the activities of implementing entities will be monitored if they are in line with the ACE’s internal regulations agreed by KDB. Reporting of complaints and allegations of impropriety, wrongdoing etc., are
conducted by PIU (Programme Implementation Unit) for Business Coordination and Sustainability under KDB Supervision, which will be established in each local FI under Component 3.

description.value: There should not be any United Nations Security Council resolutions imposing financial sanctions that would prohibit the engagement of GCF or the AE in the country or with individuals or entities under each Component of the programme. If there is any, any approvals, exemptions, licences, or other permissions are required.

mitigation.value:
KDB has ilar measures announced by the United Nations (UN) or other international organisations (e.g., World Bank, OECD, IMF, etc.), and will not deal with the countries or companies included in the list. 
In addition, it was confirmed by the internal system that Indonesia and ACE are not included in the list as of now.

description.value: There should not be any practice included in GCF and KDB prohibited practices lists, e.g., non-compliance with the E&S safeguards and gender discrimination risk as for employment, during the implementation and financing of the activities, under the GCF and KDB guidelines on prohibited practices.

mitigation.value: KDB has an internal system that controls AML/CFT and other prohibited practices, including prohinitons against E&S and Gender mainstreaming standards, and all the activities under the Programme will be monitored and supervised by KDB if any of them is in the list, based on GCF and KDB guidelines.

description.value: Regulatory barriers including lack of fiscal and non-fiscal incentives, fossil fuelled energy subsidies, etc. should be addressed for energy efficiency improvement in Indonesian industrial sector from a long term point of view. However, there is a risk that it will not improve to a satisfactory level, given that it needs to coordinate various opinions or interests between many kinds of government ministires and there may face some conflict with the economic development rationale which is one of the government’s main policy goals.

mitigation.value:
The Programme is aiming to minimize this risk thorugh Activity 3.3 under Component 3, 
In addition, it has a structure that enables a successful programme implementation without a prompt improvement of policy and regulation through GCF guarantee Cover and de-risking scheme development. 
Also, if energy efficiency project is successfully implemented and its potential economic benefit is known to policy makers, the government’s willingness to improve the energy efficiency regulatory framework is expected to increase.

rows: [A potential technical and operation risk might be caused by a lack of knowledge and competence of end beneficiaries – mainly industrial enterprise owners – surrounded by the least-developed energy efficiency market circumstances. Especially, industrial enterprises ought to adopt themselves to change into energy efficient equipment and technologies. The change necessarily requires enterprises to redefine the operation and management (O&M) process as per modification and/or replacement of technical methodology and operational mechanism.](dt.risks.risk_1.description)

[The eligibility criteria require local FIs and their borrowers (end beneficiaries) to carry out a technical assessment on underlying projects so that any potential technical and operational risk attributable to unfamiliarity and a lack of skill and knowledge could be minimised as much as possible.  The set criteria further require demonstration of a concrete O&M plan over the borrowing lifespan in order to ensure the energy efficiency system optimisation and energy saving results accordingly.  As per request from partner FIs, the Programme provides support for a technical assessment of the vulnerable group of local beneficiaries under Component 3.](dt.risks.risk_1.mitigation)

[The GCF Guarantee Facility of Component 1 would be directly exposed to the risk by its nature, up to a preagreed guarantee coverage ratio. As typically seen in a credit guarantee or insurance product, the guarantor could be also exposed to any credit risk attributable to information-asymmetry.](dt.risks.risk_3.description)

[Shortlisting and selection of local FIs takes the credit rating and relevant reputation into account. In particular, SMI and IIF, under the current discussion, are reputable private financial institutions in Indonesia and their respective credit ratings are equivalent or close to sovereign rating of the country. As such, it does not foresee the credit risk to be potentially material.  As for the FI Own Loan to be backed by the GCF guarantee Cover, the FI would share any credit risk of the relevant borrowers up to the residual portion under the guaranteed FI Own Loan. With the said mechanism, any credit risk of the final beneficiary exposed to relevant FI is not insignificant, thus the moral hazard risk to be less likely to occur.   What is more, equity injection from a final beneficiary could be told as another mitigation measure against any credit risk of borrowers.](dt.risks.risk_3.mitigation)

[There is a F/X risk of the Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) against USD because the vast majority of FI Own Loan to final beneficiaries are likely to be provided in IDR as it is the case for a typical corporate loan to domestic borrowers; however, GCF funding (Guarantee) is provided only in USD. As the GCF Credit Guarantee is denominated and made available in USD, FIs (as guarantee recipients) may be exposed to a currency mismatch risk related to the currency of defaulted debt service amounts under the FI Own Loan (in IDR, but this currency mismatch risk is limited to the case where IDR appreciates against USD.](dt.risks.risk_4.description)

[The GCF Credit Guarantee will be designed in a way which the foregoing F/X risk would be partially absorbed by the GCF and F/X risk not absorbed by GCF is borne by local FIs.  F/X risk will be regularly monitored and managed by a professional Guarantee Advisor who would be employed by KDB.](dt.risks.risk_4.mitigation)

[The programme entails multi-dimensional and multi-level legal and contractual arrangements with multiple parties, which might carry a potential legal risk in association with legality or validity and enforceability of any agreement or contract. Furthermore, dis-alignment amongst agreements and contracts governed by different jurisdictions might be another potential legal risk.](dt.risks.risk_5.description)

[In order to avoid a potential legal risk arisen by jurisdiction discrepancy, definitive agreements where KDB is a contracting party – i.e., FAA, Guarantee Agreement, and TA Service Agreement – are to be universally governed under English Law and potent disputes are to be resolved by arbitration administered by the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) in accordance with the SIAC Arbitration Rules. This is to be incorporated in the agreements.  On the other hand, all the Sub-Project Loan Agreements to be entered between a FI and each borrower are likely to be governed by the Indonesian law – the host country law. That implies that all the sub-transactions are standard corporate loan financing, which are the core business areas of local FIs with an extensive track record over decades. In that regard, the occurrence of any legal risk, potentially caused by jurisdictional discrepancy seems marginal; and even if a potential risk occurs, local FIs are deemed capable enough to tackle the legal disputes by themselves as a contacting party versed in the local legal process.  In addition, all legal agreements in the programme will be carried out with support and advice from qualified independent legal advisors, which will minimize the legal issues and controversies.](dt.risks.risk_5.mitigation)

[The GCF proceeds under the programme can also be utilised to support anti-terrorist activities, money laundering or prohibited activities policies by FIs or the final beneficiaries. Additionally, this risk of a failure to meet international standards with respect to preventing money laundering and/or financing of terrorism can present problems, such as obstacles to financial flows and/or implementation and/or payment processing. ](dt.risks.risk_6.description)

[The programme under Component 1 is supporting credit guarantees with local FIs, who will provide FI Own Loans to the final beneficiaries. As FIs were or will be selected through the proper capacity assessment by KDB including AML/CFT (KYC) assessment, final beneficiaries must also undergo due diligence according to the Sub-Project Loan Agreement between the FI and the final beneficiary. Then, it is considered that such related risk has been substantially mitigated.  Also, Indonesia has the national regulatory system to monitor relevant issues of the financial institutions under the purview of central bank. Moreover, the potential Executing Entity under Component 1 has an internal regulation and policy about their investment activities, so the final beneficiaries’ activities under the programme will be properly screened and monitored.  Under Components 2 and 3, AML/CFT assessment on the Executing Entity (ACE) is already completed by KDB, and the activities of implementing entities will be monitored if they are in line with the ACE’s internal regulations agreed by KDB. Reporting of complaints and allegations of impropriety, wrongdoing etc., are  conducted by PIU (Programme Implementation Unit) for Business Coordination and Sustainability under KDB Supervision, which will be established in each local FI under Component 3.](dt.risks.risk_6.mitigation)

[There should not be any United Nations Security Council resolutions imposing financial sanctions that would prohibit the engagement of GCF or the AE in the country or with individuals or entities under each Component of the programme. If there is any, any approvals, exemptions, licences, or other permissions are required.](dt.risks.risk_7.description)

[KDB has ilar measures announced by the United Nations (UN) or other international organisations (e.g., World Bank, OECD, IMF, etc.), and will not deal with the countries or companies included in the list.   In addition, it was confirmed by the internal system that Indonesia and ACE are not included in the list as of now.](dt.risks.risk_7.mitigation)
[There should not be any practice included in GCF and KDB prohibited practices lists, e](dt.risks.risk_8.name)

[There should not be any practice included in GCF and KDB prohibited practices lists, e.g., non-compliance with the E&S safeguards and gender discrimination risk as for employment, during the implementation and financing of the activities, under the GCF and KDB guidelines on prohibited practices. ](dt.risks.risk_8.description)

[KDB has an internal system that controls AML/CFT and other prohibited practices, including prohinitons against E&S and Gender mainstreaming standards, and all the activities under the Programme will be monitored and supervised by KDB if any of them is in the list, based on GCF and KDB guidelines.](dt.risks.risk_8.mitigation)

[Regulatory barriers including lack of fiscal and non-fiscal incentives, fossil fuelled energy subsidies, etc. should be addressed for energy efficiency improvement in Indonesian industrial sector from a long term point of view. However, there is a risk that it will not improve to a satisfactory level, given that it needs to coordinate various opinions or interests between many kinds of government ministires and there may face some conflict with the economic development rationale which is one of the government’s main policy goals. ](dt.risks.risk_9.description)

[The Programme is aiming to minimize this risk thorugh Activity 3.3 under Component 3,   In addition, it has a structure that enables a successful programme implementation without a prompt improvement of policy and regulation through GCF guarantee Cover and de-risking scheme development.   Also, if energy efficiency project is successfully implemented and its potential economic benefit is known to policy makers, the government’s willingness to improve the energy efficiency regulatory framework is expected to increase. ](dt.risks.risk_9.mitigation)
